title: AWS Batch on Fargate, Step Functions and Lambda: who does what

blocks.text: 12.5.2 AWS Batch on Fargate, Step Functions and Lambda: Who Does What

The GridCap service now has an image (lesson 12.5.1). In lesson 12.4.2 its solves ran on worker threads inside the API's own process, one machine for everything. On the medium portfolio a solve can take many minutes; in the planning cycle's last week, a dozen planners submit scenarios within an hour. The API should answer in milliseconds whatever the solver is doing, and each solve should get its own CPUs, its own memory and its own time limit. AWS offers several services that can run code. This lesson gives each part of a run to the one built for it: **AWS Batch on Fargate** runs the solve, **Step Functions** watches it, **Lambda** does the short clean-up, S3 holds the data (lesson 12.5.3), and the API keeps answering. (GridCap is fictional; no number in it is real.)

Everything runnable here talks to **moto**, a library that imitates AWS inside the Python process (lesson 12.5.4 covers it). No AWS account is used, and the account id in every ARN, `123456789012`, is moto's placeholder.
The Model
The worker solves the model of lesson 12.2.1 from a validated snapshot, unchanged. It is restated here whole.

**Sets.** $`Y`$ the plan's years, in order; $`P`$ the candidate projects; $`T_i`$ the start years of project $`i`$: the years $`t`$ with $`e_i \le t \le l_i`$ and $`t + d_i - 1 \le \max Y`$; $`M \subseteq P`$ the must-do projects; $`\mathcal{G}`$ the alternative groups; $`C \subseteq P`$ the child projects, each with parent $`p(c)`$ and lag $`L_c`$; $`Q`$ the programs, with $`q(i)`$ the program of project $`i`$; $`R`$ the regions, with $`r(i)`$ the region of project $`i`$.

**Parameters.** $`e_i, l_i`$, the earliest and latest start years; $`c_{i,k}`$, what project $`i`$ spends in its $`k`$-th year of work ($k), $`d_i`$ its years of work, and $`\text{capex}_i = \sum_k c_{i,k}`$; $`\text{npv}_{i,t}`$ ($k); $`m_i`$, crew-months per year of work; $`B_y`$, the budget of year $`y`$ ($k); $`K_{q,y}`$, the crew-months of program $`q`$ in year $`y`$; $`\text{floor}_r`$, the least region $`r`$ receives over the plan ($k).
**Variables.** $`x_{i,t} \in \{0, 1\}`$ for every $`i \in P`$ and $`t \in T_i`$: project $`i`$ starts in year $`t`$.
**Objective.**
\max \; \sum_{i \in P} \sum_{t \in T_i} \text{npv}_{i,t}\, x_{i,t}
**Constraints.**

\begin{aligned}
\sum_{t \in T_i} x_{i,t} &\le 1 && \forall i \in P \setminus M && \text{(once}_i) \\
\sum_{t \in T_i} x_{i,t} &= 1 && \forall i \in M && \text{(must}_i) \\
\sum_{i \in g} \sum_{t \in T_i} x_{i,t} &\le 1 && \forall g \in \mathcal{G} && \text{(alt}_g) \\
\sum_{u \in T_c,\, u \le t} x_{c,u} &\le \sum_{s \in T_{p(c)},\, s \le t - L_c} x_{p(c),s} && \forall c \in C,\ t \in T_c && \text{(after}_{c,t}) \\
\sum_{i \in P} \sum_{t \in T_i,\, 0 \le y - t < d_i} c_{i,\,y-t}\, x_{i,t} &\le B_y && \forall y \in Y && \text{(budget}_y) \\
\sum_{i:\, q(i) = q} \ \sum_{t \in T_i,\, 0 \le y - t < d_i} m_i\, x_{i,t} &\le K_{q,y} && \forall q \in Q,\ y \in Y && \text{(crews}_{q,y}) \\
\sum_{i:\, r(i) = r} \ \sum_{t \in T_i} \text{capex}_i\, x_{i,t} &\ge \text{floor}_r && \forall r \in R && \text{(floor}_r)
\end{aligned}
What changes is where it runs: in a container started for one run, with a time limit from the run's settings (lesson 12.5.1). On GridCap small it solves to an NPV of $22,741k, as in lesson 12.2.2.
Each Service Does the Part It Is Built For
A run has five parts, and each needs something different:

rows: the API (lesson 12.4.2), with the SQLite run index (lesson 12.5.3)
keep the snapshot and the result
minutes to hours, several CPUs, gigabytes of memory
wait for the solve, react when it fails
runs as long as the job, retries, branches on errors
write a `failed` result when the job never could
a few seconds of code, on demand

blocks.text: The choice follows from documented limits:

items: **Lambda runs a function for at most 900 seconds (15 minutes)**, with up to 10,240 MB of memory. A solve has no such bound: the medium portfolio with a long limit, or the large one, can take an hour. A function stopped at 15 minutes leaves no result at all. So Lambda never solves; it does the small glue steps, which finish in seconds.

**AWS Batch** runs a container as a **job**: it queues jobs, starts each one when capacity is free, and records its status until it ends as `SUCCEEDED` or `FAILED`. On **Fargate**, AWS supplies the machine: no servers to patch or scale, and each job gets exactly the vCPUs and memory its definition asks for. A job's own timeout (at least 60 seconds) is its only time bound.

**Step Functions** runs a **state machine**: a JSON definition of steps (states) and the moves between them. A Standard workflow may run for up to a year, so it can wait for the longest solve. It is the part that knows what to do when the job fails.

blocks.text: The API does none of the waiting. It stores the snapshot, starts the run, writes one index row, and answers 202 Accepted as in lesson 12.4.2. Later polls read the index, and the result object in S3.
A Job Definition Fixes the Image, Size, Timeout and Retries; a Submission Names the Run

Batch separates what every solve shares from what one run needs. The **job definition** is the template, registered once (by Terraform in lesson 12.5.5): the image, its command, its size, the two roles, a timeout and a retry count. `batch_stack.py` registers it in moto:

def job_definition(execution_role: str, job_role: str) -> dict:
    """The solve job's definition: the image, its command, its size, its timeout and its retries."""
    return dict(
        jobDefinitionName="gridcap-solve",
        type="container",
        platformCapabilities=["FARGATE"],
        containerProperties={
            "image": IMAGE,
            "command": ["python", "-c", "import solve_worker; raise SystemExit(solve_worker.main())"],
            "executionRoleArn": execution_role,      # lets Fargate pull the image and write logs
            "jobRoleArn": job_role,                  # what the solve itself may do in S3
            "resourceRequirements": [{"type": "VCPU", "value": "2"}, {"type": "MEMORY", "value": "8192"}],
            "environment": [{"name": "RESULT_BUCKET", "value": "gridcap-runs-example"},
                            {"name": "PYTHON_CPU_COUNT", "value": "2"}],
            "networkConfiguration": {"assignPublicIp": "DISABLED"},
        },
        timeout={"attemptDurationSeconds": 3600},
        retryStrategy={"attempts": 2},
    )

The fields the AWS Batch documentation requires for Fargate are all here: `platformCapabilities` of `FARGATE`, the `container` type, an **execution role** (what Fargate itself uses to pull the image and write logs), and the size as `resourceRequirements`. The **job role** is separate: it is what the solve's own code may do, read snapshots and write results, and nothing else (lesson 12.5.5 writes it). `assignPublicIp` is `DISABLED`; the documentation says that a job whose subnet has no NAT gateway needs it `ENABLED` for outbound network access, so this design assumes subnets with a NAT gateway.
**Fargate sizes come in fixed pairs.** A job asks for vCPUs and memory, and Fargate accepts only these combinations (from the AWS Batch API reference for `ResourceRequirement`):
So "1 vCPU and 12 GB" is not a size: it becomes 2 vCPUs (the smallest that allows 12,288 MiB), or the memory comes down. The worker's 2 vCPUs and 8,192 MiB is a valid pair.
**A submission names one run.** `submit_solve` sends what changes per run, as environment overrides that the worker's settings read (lesson 12.5.1):

def submit_solve(batch, stack: Stack, run_id: str, digest: str, time_limit_s: int) -> str:
    """Submit one solve job; return Batch's job id. The run id doubles as the job's name."""
    job = batch.submit_job(
        jobName=run_id,
        jobQueue=stack.queue,
        jobDefinition=stack.definition,
        containerOverrides={"environment": [
            {"name": "RUN_ID", "value": run_id},
            {"name": "SNAPSHOT_DIGEST", "value": digest},
            {"name": "TIME_LIMIT_S", "value": str(time_limit_s)},
        ]},
        timeout={"attemptDurationSeconds": max(60, time_limit_s + 600)},
    )
    return job["jobId"]
Two choices to notice:

items: **The job's timeout is longer than the solver's limit.** The solver stops itself at its limit and writes a `time_limit` result with its best plan. Batch's timeout is the backstop for a job that hangs: the documentation says a job stopped by its timeout is not retried, and it writes nothing. If the two were equal, Batch could kill the worker in the seconds it needs to write the result, and the planner would lose a plan the solver had found. Ten minutes of margin covers pulling the image, reading the snapshot and writing the result.

**Batch has no idempotency token.** `SubmitJob` takes no client token, so the same call sent twice starts two jobs. The next section puts the run's start behind Step Functions, whose execution name does deduplicate.

blocks.text: `start_run` does a run's three writes in an order where each refers only to what already exists: the snapshot first, then the job that reads it, then the index row that points at both:

digest = store.put_snapshot(snap)
    job_id = submit_solve(batch, stack, run_id, digest, time_limit_s)
    run_index.record_submitted(conn, run_id, digest, job_id)
`batch_submit.py` starts run `run-0007` on GridCap small with a 60-second limit, then reads the job back from Batch:

job name: run-0007 | queue: job-queue/gridcap-solves
job definition: job-definition/gridcap-solve:1
environment overrides: ['RUN_ID', 'SNAPSHOT_DIGEST', 'TIME_LIMIT_S']
job timeout: 660 s for a 60 s solver limit
Batch says: SUCCEEDED | index says: submitted
after the worker ran, index says: optimal
status optimal, NPV $22,741k, result at results/730c8b40b1eb...

Read the fifth line carefully. moto, configured as this module configures it, does not start containers: it marks every job `SUCCEEDED` without running anything. So "Batch says SUCCEEDED" while no result exists, and the index rightly still says `submitted`: a poll trusts the result object, not the job's status. The program then does what the container would have done, running the worker with the environment Batch recorded for the job, and the next poll finds the result: optimal, $22,741k, the base plan.
<!-- practice 1 -->
Step Functions Waits for the Job and Catches What the Worker Cannot

The worker writes a result for every way a solve can end (lesson 12.4.2's statuses). But some failures happen outside the worker: the image cannot be pulled, the container runs out of memory, or Batch's timeout stops it. Then no result is written, and a planner would poll `submitted` forever. A state machine closes that gap. Its definition is read-along JSON in the Amazon States Language, `deploy/stepfunctions/solve-run.asl.json`:

items: **`batch:submitJob.sync`** is Step Functions' "run a job" pattern: it submits the Batch job and waits until the job finishes, then moves on. A field ending in `.$` takes its value from the execution's input by a JSONPath (`$.run_id`).
**`Catch`** sends any error (`States.ALL`) to `RecordFailure`, with the error added to the input under `error` (that is what `ResultPath` does in a catcher).

blocks.text: How a state reacts to an error, as the Step Functions documentation describes it: the state's `Retry` list is tried first, and the first retrier whose `ErrorEquals` names the error retries the state, up to its `MaxAttempts` (3 unless set; 0 means never), waiting `IntervalSeconds` and then multiplying the wait by `BackoffRate`. When no retrier matches, or the matching one has used its attempts, the `Catch` list is scanned in order and the first catcher that names the error decides the next state. With neither, the whole execution fails. Two names are wildcards: `States.ALL` matches any error and must stand alone, in the last retrier or catcher; `States.TaskFailed` matches any error except `States.Timeout`, which a task reports when it runs past its own `TimeoutSeconds`.
`step_functions.py` reads the definition and prints each state, where it goes next and where an error goes:

Solve          Task     batch:submitJob.sync next Solved         on error ['RecordFailure']
RecordFailure  Task     lambda:invoke        next Failed         on error -
Solved         Succeed                       next end: Succeed   on error -
Failed         Fail                          next end: Fail      on error -
`RecordFailure` calls a Lambda function, the one short task in the design. It writes a `failed` result in the run's place, unless the worker wrote one after all:

try:
        key = store.put_result(event["snapshot_digest"], event["run_id"], record)
    except FileExistsError:                       # the worker wrote a result after all; keep it
        key = None

Its retry rule in the definition retries Lambda's own transient errors (`Lambda.ServiceException`, `Lambda.SdkClientException`), so a second call must be harmless. It is, because a result is written only if none exists (S3's conditional write, lesson 12.5.3). moto stores a state machine but runs none of its states, so the program calls the function itself, twice, with the input the catcher would pass. The key it returns has the shape `results/<digest>/<run>.json`; the program prints the 64-character digest cut to its first 12 characters and `...`:

**The execution's name is the run id, and that makes starting a run idempotent.** The Step Functions API reference says that for a Standard workflow, starting an execution with the name and input of one that is still running returns that execution instead of starting another, and that the same name with different input is refused with `ExecutionAlreadyExists`. The API's retry of a "start run" call therefore cannot start a second solve. moto behaves the same way here:

first = sfn.start_execution(stateMachineArn=machine, name=run["run_id"], input=json.dumps(run))
    again = sfn.start_execution(stateMachineArn=machine, name=run["run_id"], input=json.dumps(run))

same name, same input -> same execution: True
same name, other input -> ExecutionAlreadyExists

So in production the API starts the state machine with the run's input rather than calling `submit_job` itself; `submit_solve` above is what the `Solve` state does on its behalf, and is the call this module tests. The Step Functions documentation adds that a closed execution's name is refused too, and can be reused only 90 days after it closed, so a run id is never recycled.
<!-- practice 2 -->
Summary

items: **Each service does the part it is built for.** The API answers; S3 keeps data; Batch on Fargate solves; Step Functions waits and catches; Lambda (900 s at most) does short glue, never the solve.
**A job definition fixes the image, size, timeout and retries; a submission names the run.** Fargate accepts only listed vCPU and memory pairs. The job's timeout exceeds the solver's limit.
**Step Functions waits for the job and catches what the worker cannot.** `submitJob.sync` waits; a `Catch` routes a failed job to a Lambda that writes a `failed` result once.
**Batch has no idempotency token; a Step Functions execution name does.** Name the execution after the run.
**moto marks Batch jobs `SUCCEEDED` without running them.** Trust the result object, not the job status.

blocks.text: Reference

rows: one execution of a state machine
the template: image, command, size, roles, timeout, retries
status and recorded settings of jobs
submit a Batch job and wait for it
take a value from the input (JSONPath)
on any error, add it to the input and go on
retry the state on those errors; tried before `Catch`

blocks.text: **Further reading:** OR-Tools, the [MathOpt overview](https://developers.google.com/optimization/math_opt) (the solver the worker calls); AWS Lambda, [Lambda quotas](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/gettingstarted-limits.html) (900 s, 10,240 MB); AWS Batch, [Fargate job definitions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/batch/latest/userguide/fargate-job-definitions.html), [Job definition parameters](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/batch/latest/userguide/job_definition_parameters.html) (execution and job roles, `assignPublicIp`), [ResourceRequirement](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/batch/latest/APIReference/API_ResourceRequirement.html) (the Fargate pairs), [RegisterJobDefinition](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/batch/latest/APIReference/API_RegisterJobDefinition.html) (a timed-out job is not retried; 60 s minimum), [RetryStrategy](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/batch/latest/APIReference/API_RetryStrategy.html) and [SubmitJob](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/batch/latest/APIReference/API_SubmitJob.html); AWS Step Functions, [Run AWS Batch workloads](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/connect-batch.html) (`submitJob.sync`), [Invoke Lambda](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/connect-lambda.html), [Handling errors](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/concepts-error-handling.html) (`Retry`, `Catch`, `States.ALL`), [StartExecution](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/apireference/API_StartExecution.html) (idempotent names) and [quotas](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/service-quotas.html); moto, [Configuration](https://docs.getmoto.org/en/latest/docs/configuration/index.html) (Batch without Docker) and [Step Functions](https://docs.getmoto.org/en/latest/docs/services/stepfunctions.html).
Challenges

items: A planner cancels a run. Which service do you ask to stop it, and what should the index say afterwards? (Step Functions' `.sync` pattern can also stop the job it started.)
The large portfolio needs 16 vCPUs. Write the `containerOverrides` that ask for it, with the smallest memory Fargate allows at that size, and the matching `PYTHON_CPU_COUNT`.
A run's state machine fails in `RecordFailure` itself, after three retries. What does a poll show, and how would you find such runs?

blocks.text: Design Note: Why the Index Is Not Written by the Cloud

The index is a SQLite file on the API's own disk (lesson 12.5.3), so neither Batch nor Lambda writes to it: they would need a path into the API's machine. Instead, everything the cloud produces lands in S3 under a key the API can compute from the run (`results/<digest>/<run>.json`), and the API records it on the next poll. The cloud parts never need to know the index exists, and the index can be rebuilt from S3 if its file is lost.
The Full Programs

Each snippet above is part of a complete program, and each program printed the output the lesson shows. Open one to read it whole, change it, and run it again: Run starts the program on your copy of the code, so the course's own files never change.

**batch_submit.py.** Creates the Batch stack in moto, starts a run, reads the job back, and runs the worker as the container would (*A Job Definition Fixes the Image, Size, Timeout and Retries*). *Try:* Submit with `time_limit_s=10`. Predict the job's timeout.

**step_functions.py.** Reads the state machine, starts it twice under one name, and calls the failure function twice (*Step Functions Waits for the Job*). *Try:* Start a third execution named `run-0008` with the first input. Predict whether it is refused.

**batch_stack.py** creates the network, roles, compute environment, queue and job definition; **submitter.py** submits a solve and starts a run; **record_failure.py** is the Lambda function; **run_index.py** and **s3_store.py** are lesson 12.5.3's index and store.
